query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The mechanical and thermoelastic behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) is primarily governed by the heterogeneous lattice strain and the resulting dislocation behaviors, which lead to strengthening mechanisms and improved strength-ductility synergy.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) with a face-centered cubic (FCC) or hexagonal close-packed (HCP) crystal structure
generation.intervention: Variation of alloy composition, temperature, and strain rate
generation.conditions: High-temperature environment (T ≥ 1000 °C) and slow strain rates
generation.structural_mediator: Heterogeneous lattice strain and dislocation behaviors
generation.mechanism: Strengthening mechanisms due to dislocation interactions and lattice distortion
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strength-ductility synergy and enhanced mechanical properties at high temperatures
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 1000 °C - 1500 °C, strain rates: 10^-4 s^-1 - 10^-2 s^-1
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between lattice strain, dislocation behaviors, and mechanical properties is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile deformation experiments at slow strain rates and high temperatures, with in-situ neutron diffraction and transmission electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heterogeneous lattice strain and dislocation behaviors are not correlated with the strengthening mechanisms and improved strength-ductility synergy, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: AbstractIn order to find more excellent structural materials resistant to radiation damage, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have been developed due to their characteristics of limited point defect diffusion such as lattice distortion and slow diffusion. Specially, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) that can adapt to a high-temperature environment are badly needed. In this study, TiZrHfNbMo0.1 RHEAs are selected for irradiation and nanoindentation experiments. We combined the mechanistic model for the depth-dependent hardness of ion-irradiated metals and the introduction of the scale factor f to modify the irradiation-hardening model in order to better describe the nanoindentation indentation process in the irradiated layer. Finally, it can be found that, with the increase in irradiation dose, a more serious lattice distortion caused by a higher defect density limits the expansion of the plastic zone.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical properties, ion irradiation, indentation size effect, plastic zone

Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. The so-called high-entropy alloys based on the refractory elements (refractory high-entropy alloys, RHEAs) are considered as candidates for high-temperature applications [,,,,]. Some of them have high strength at T ≥ 1000 °C and thus can potentially operate at higher temperatures than commercial nickel-based superalloys [,,,,,,,,,]. Some RHEAs are sufficiently ductile at room temperature even in tension [,,,,] and can be cold rolled [,,,]. However, refractory elements and their alloys are generally vulnerable to oxidation. A number of studies focused on oxidation behavior of different RHEAs [,,,,,,,,,,] have demonstrated that some of them possess much better oxidation resistance than conventional refractory alloys; however, the oxidation behavior strongly depended on the alloy composition and testing conditions. Note that the vast majority of the performed research was conducted at temperatures of T ≥ 1000 °C [,,,,,,].

Our results reveal that the heterogeneous lattice strain causes unusual dislocation behaviors (i.e., multiple kinks/jogs and bidirectional cross slips), resulting in the strengthening mechanisms that underpin the strength-ductility synergy. The outcome of our research sheds important insights into the design of strong yet ductile distorted crystalline solids, such as high-entropy alloys and high-entropy ceramics.
